# Map recorded property offences per 100,000 residents in Polish counties in 2023.

# Load packages
pacman::p_load(here, httr2, leaflet, readxl, sf, tidyverse)


# Load data --------------------------------------------------------------------

# Download property offence counts into the workspace
request(
  "https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/poland_property_crime_counts.xlsx"
) |>
  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "poland_property_crime_counts.xlsx"))

# Download population counts into the workspace
request("https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/poland_population.tsv") |>
  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "poland_population.tsv"))

# Download powiat boundaries into the workspace
request(
  "https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/poland_powiat_boundaries.gpkg"
) |>
  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "poland_powiat_boundaries.gpkg"))

# Read property offence counts, keeping geographic codes as text
property_crime <- here("data", "raw", "poland_property_crime_counts.xlsx") |>
  read_excel() |>
  # Select counts for 2023 only
  filter(rok == 2023)

# Read population counts, keeping geographic codes as text
population <- here("data", "raw", "poland_population.tsv") |>
  read_tsv() |>
  # Select population counts for 2023 only
  filter(rok == 2023)

# Read powiat boundaries as an SF object
powiats <- here("data", "raw", "poland_powiat_boundaries.gpkg") |>
  read_sf()


# Wrangle data -----------------------------------------------------------------

# Join 2023 counts to county boundaries and calculate incidence rates
property_crime_rate <- powiats |>
  # Join property offence counts using the common territorial code
  left_join(property_crime, by = join_by(jpt_kod_je == kod_teryt)) |>
  # Join population counts using the same territorial code
  left_join(
    select(population, kod_teryt, ludnosc),
    by = join_by(jpt_kod_je == kod_teryt)
  ) |>
  # Calculate property offences per 100,000 residents
  mutate(rate = przestepstwa_przeciwko_mieniu / ludnosc * 100000) |>
  # Transform coordinates for the interactive map
  st_transform("EPSG:4326")


# Create map -------------------------------------------------------------------

# Create a sequential colour palette for property crime rates
property_crime_colours <- colorNumeric(
  palette = "Reds",
  domain = pull(property_crime_rate, "rate")
)

# Create an interactive map of property crime rates
leaflet(property_crime_rate) |>
  # Add a light base map
  addProviderTiles("OpenStreetMap.Mapnik") |>
  # Colour powiats by rate and label them with their names and rates
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~ property_crime_colours(rate),
    fillOpacity = 0.75,
    label = ~ paste0(
      jpt_nazwa,
      ": ",
      round(rate, 1),
      " property offences per 100,000 residents in 2023"
    ),
    weight = 1,
    color = "black"
  ) |>
  # Add a legend identifying the place, year and rate units
  addLegend(
    pal = property_crime_colours,
    values = ~rate,
    title = htmltools::HTML(
      "Property crimes per<br>100,000 residents<br>in Poland, 2023"
    )
  ) |>
  # Add an inset map that readers can minimise
  addMiniMap(toggleDisplay = TRUE) |>
  # Credit the providers of the statistical data and processed boundaries
  addControl(
    html = paste0(
      "Statistics: Statistics Poland (CC BY 4.0).<br>",
      "Boundaries: Head Office of Geodesy and Cartography (GUGiK),<br>",
      "National Register of Boundaries (PRG)."
    ),
    position = "bottomleft"
  )

# Map recorded stalking incidents per 100,000 residents in Queensland in 2018.

# Load packages
pacman::p_load(here, httr2, sf, sfhotspot, tidyverse)


# Load data --------------------------------------------------------------------

# Download the original data into the workspace
request("https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/qld_stalking.xlsx") |>
  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "qld_stalking.xlsx"))
request("https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/qld_population.csv.gz") |>
  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "qld_population.csv.gz"))
request(
  "https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/qld_police_divisions.gpkg"
) |>
  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "qld_police_divisions.gpkg"))

# Read local data and select stalking counts for 2018
# No need to specify the `sheet` argument in `read_excel()` because the Excel
# file only has one sheet
stalking <- here("data", "raw", "qld_stalking.xlsx") |>
  readxl::read_excel() |>
  filter(year == 2018)
population <- here("data", "raw", "qld_population.csv.gz") |>
  read_csv()
divisions <- here("data", "raw", "qld_police_divisions.gpkg") |>
  read_sf()


# Wrangle data -----------------------------------------------------------------

# Join data and calculate rate
stalking_rate <- divisions |>
  left_join(population, by = join_by(division == police_division)) |>
  left_join(stalking, by = join_by(division)) |>
  mutate(rate = stalking / population * 100000)

# Pimpama has no matching population, so its rate remains NA.
# Keep it on the map in grey rather than treating missing data as zero.

# Find divisions with highest stalking rate
stalking_rate_highest <- slice_max(
  stalking_rate,
  rate,
  n = 10,
  with_ties = FALSE
)


# Create map -------------------------------------------------------------------

stalking_map <- hotspot_map(
  stalking_rate,
  mapping = aes(fill = rate),
  basemap_type = "cartolight",
  caption = str_glue(
    "Map produced by Joe Bloggs on {today()}\n",
    "Offences: Queensland Police Service (CC BY 4.0)\n",
    "Population and boundaries: Queensland Government\n",
    "Grey: rate cannot be calculated because population data unavailable"
  ),
  alpha = 0.75,
  linewidth = 0.25
) +
  # Add thicker boundaries for 10 divisions with highest rates
  geom_sf(
    data = stalking_rate_highest,
    colour = "black",
    fill = NA,
    linewidth = 0.75
  ) +
  scale_fill_distiller(direction = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Recorded stalking rates in Queensland",
    subtitle = str_glue(
      "Ten police divisions with the highest rates are highlighted"
    ),
    fill = "stalking incidents\nper 100,000 people\nin 2018"
  ) +
  theme(
    # Slightly lower the legend in the visual hierarchy by giving it a
    # background that is white and semi-transparent
    legend.background = element_rect(colour = NA, fill = rgb(1, 1, 1, 0.75)),
    # Base legend position on the top-right corner of the legend, which makes
    # moving the legend to the top-right corner easier
    legend.justification = c(1, 1),
    # Add some padding around the legend
    legend.margin = margin(6, 9, 9, 9),
    # Move the legend almost to the top-right corner of the map, since this is
    # the area of the map with no content in it
    legend.position = "inside",
    legend.position.inside = c(0.95, 0.98),
    # Make the legend title slightly smaller, again reducing its prominence
    legend.title = element_text(size = 10),
    # Left-align the caption
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0),
    # Add some space above and below the plot subtitle
    plot.subtitle = element_text(margin = margin(6, 0, 6, 0)),
    # Make the plot title larger and bold to move it up the visual hierarchy
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16)
  )


# Save map ---------------------------------------------------------------------

# Create map that is 2000px x 2000px
ggsave(
  filename = here("output", "queensland_stalking_rate_map_2018.jpg"),
  plot = stalking_map,
  width = 2000,
  height = 2000,
  units = "px"
)

# This script produces a map of concentrations of calls to opioid overdoses in
# Tempe, Arizona, since January 2020. Run in the crime_mapping workspace.

# PREPARE ----------------------------------------------------------------------

## Load packages ----
pacman::p_load(ggspatial, here, httr2, sf, sfhotspot, tidyverse)


## Load data ----

# All data layers should be harmonised to use EPSG:6404 since this uses metres
# and covers the central part of Arizona

# Download the original data into the workspace
request("https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/tempe_opioid_calls.csv") |>
  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "tempe_opioid_calls.csv"))
request(
  "https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/tempe_character_areas.gml"
) |>
  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "tempe_character_areas.gml"))

# Read local calls data, keep calls since January 2020 and transform coordinates
incidents <- here("data", "raw", "tempe_opioid_calls.csv") |>
  read_csv() |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  filter(incident_date >= ymd("2020-01-01")) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = "EPSG:4326") |>
  st_transform("EPSG:6404")

# Read the local city boundary and use the same coordinate reference system
character_areas <- here("data", "raw", "tempe_character_areas.gml") |>
  read_sf() |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  st_transform("EPSG:6404") |>
  # Some of the character areas have very long names which would not fit easily
  # on the map, so we abbreviate them first
  mutate(
    label = case_when(
      area_number == 1 ~ "North Tempe",
      area_number == 2 ~ "Double Butte",
      area_number == 3 ~ "Downtown",
      area_number == 7 ~ "The Lakes",
      area_number == 8 ~ "South Tempe",
      # If the area number is not specified above, use the existing area name
      TRUE ~ area_name
    )
  )


# WRANGLE ----------------------------------------------------------------------

# Estimate call density on a 200-metre grid, then clip it to the city boundary.
# Some recorded calls fall outside the boundary; a warning may be produced.
# Clipping limits the displayed density surface to the city rather than
# interpreting those approximate coordinates as exact locations.
incidents_kde <- incidents |>
  hotspot_kde(
    grid = hotspot_grid(character_areas, cell_size = 150),
    bandwidth_adjust = 0.33,
    quiet = TRUE
  ) |>
  hotspot_isoband(breaks = 10, quiet = TRUE) |>
  hotspot_clip(character_areas, quiet = TRUE)


# VISUALISE --------------------------------------------------------------------

# Create map
tempe_opioid_map <- hotspot_map(
  incidents_kde,
  basemap_type = "cartolight",
  caption = str_glue(
    "Author: Joe Bloggs, Date produced: {today()}\n",
    "Calls and character areas: City of Tempe (CC BY)\n",
    "Locations are approximate"
  )
) +
  # Add character area boundaries
  geom_sf(data = character_areas, colour = "grey50", fill = NA) +
  # Add character area labels
  geom_sf_label(
    aes(label = str_wrap(label, 10)),
    data = character_areas,
    alpha = 0.5,
    fill = "white",
    lineheight = 1,
    linewidth = 0,
    size = 2.5
  ) +
  # Add scale bar
  annotation_scale(width_hint = 1 / 5, style = "ticks", location = "bl") +
  labs(
    title = "Calls for suspected opioid overdoses in Tempe",
    subtitle = str_glue(
      "Calls to emergency medical services, ",
      "{format(min(pull(incidents, 'incident_date')), '%b %Y')} to ",
      "{format(max(pull(incidents, 'incident_date')), '%b %Y')}"
    ),
    fill = "density of\ncalls"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 6),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9, margin = margin(6, 0, 6, 0))
  )

# Save map
ggsave(
  here("output", "tempe_opioid_calls.jpg"),
  plot = tempe_opioid_map,
  width = 2000,
  height = 2000,
  units = "px"
)

# Map the density of recorded fatal shootings in NYC in 2019,
# excluding Staten Island.

# Note: both datasets will be harmonised to use EPSG:6538 for use with
# `hotspot_kde()`

## Load packages and data ------------------------------------------------------

# Load packages
pacman::p_load(ggspatial, here, httr2, sf, sfhotspot, tidyverse)

# Download the original data into the workspace
request("https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/nyc_shootings.csv") |>
  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "nyc_shootings.csv"))
request("https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/nyc_precincts.gpkg") |>
  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "nyc_precincts.gpkg"))

# Read local shootings data and select fatal shootings in 2019
shootings <- here("data", "raw", "nyc_shootings.csv") |>
  read_csv() |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  filter(murder == TRUE) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = "EPSG:4326") |>
  st_transform("EPSG:6538")

# Load NYC police precincts data
precincts <- here("data", "raw", "nyc_precincts.gpkg") |>
  read_sf() |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  # Filter out precincts in Staten Island, since there are very few fatal
  # shootings there and it takes up a lot of space due to the position of Staten
  # Island relative to the rest of NYC
  filter(precinct <= 119) |>
  st_transform("EPSG:6538")


## Wrangle data ----------------------------------------------------------------

# Calculate KDE
shootings_kde <- shootings |>
  hotspot_kde(
    grid = hotspot_grid(precincts, cell_size = 400),
    bandwidth_adjust = 0.33,
    quiet = TRUE
  ) |>
  hotspot_clip(precincts, quiet = TRUE)


## Make map --------------------------------------------------------------------

shootings_map <- hotspot_map(
  shootings_kde,
  basemap_type = "cartolight",
  caption = str_glue(
    "Author: Joe Bloggs, Date produced: {today()}\n",
    "Shootings: New York City Police Department\n",
    "Boundaries: City of New York (CC BY 3.0 AU)"
  )
) +
  geom_sf(data = precincts, colour = "grey33", fill = NA) +
  geom_sf_label(
    aes(label = scales::ordinal(precinct)),
    data = precincts,
    alpha = 0.5,
    colour = "grey33",
    fill = "white",
    size = 2.5,
    linewidth = NA
  ) +
  annotation_scale(width_hint = 1 / 5, style = "ticks", location = "br") +
  labs(
    title = "Density of recorded fatal shootings in New York City",
    subtitle = "Fatal shootings recorded by NYC Police, 2019, excluding Staten Island",
    fill = "density of\nshootings"
  ) +
  theme(
    # We're going to overlay the legend on the map, so we should give the
    # legend a solid background
    legend.background = element_rect(colour = NA, fill = "#F2F2F2"),
    # Use the top-right corner of the legend as the anchor point for determining
    # its position
    legend.justification = c(1, 1),
    # Create a margin around the legend, since it has a solid background
    legend.margin = margin(6, 6, 6, 6),
    # Move the top-right corner of the legend to be very near the top-right
    # corner of the map
    legend.position = "inside",
    legend.position.inside = c(0.98, 0.98),
    # Make the legend and title smaller to reduce their visual prominence
    legend.text = element_text(size = rel(0.7)),
    legend.title = element_text(size = rel(0.8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = rel(0.8), margin = margin(3, 0, 6, 0)),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey45", size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0)
  )

# Save the finished map in the workspace output folder
ggsave(
  here("output", "nyc_fatal_shootings_2019.png"),
  plot = shootings_map,
  width = 210,
  height = 210,
  units = "mm"
)

10

11

st_as_sf() tells R that the numbers in the longitude and latitude columns in the data represent points on the Earth’s surface. coords specifies which columns contain the x and y coordinates, in that order. crs = "EPSG:4326" identifies which coordinate reference system R should use to translate the numbers in those columns into geographic locations. 12

# Load NYC police precincts data
13precincts <- here("data", "raw", "nyc_precincts.gpkg") |>
14  read_sf() |>
15  janitor::clean_names() |>
16  # Filter out precincts in Staten Island, since there are very few fatal
  # shootings there and it takes up a lot of space due to the position of Staten
  # Island relative to the rest of NYC
17  filter(precinct <= 119) |>
18  st_transform("EPSG:6538")

13

here() again specifies which file we are going to load data from. The result of this whole pipeline will be stored as precincts.

14

read_sf() reads the spatial file containing the precinct boundaries. Since this file is in a spatial data format (in this case, a geopackage), it includes the information R needs about the geometry and CRS, so we do not need to then use st_as_sf(). See Reading spatial data.

15

Clean the column names using the same convention as before.

16

At this point the code makes an important decision, to exclude Staten Island from the analysis. This is a judgement call on the part of the person who wrote this code – including Staten Island in the map would also have been a reasonable choice. The reason that this code excludes Staten Island is that has very few fatal shootings but is geographically large, so it would occupy a large proportion of the map if left included. Readers of crime analysis products such as crime maps are usually (although not always) interested in the areas with most crime, so excluding Staten Island allows for a more focused analysis of the areas with the highest crime rates. However, this depends very much on the intended audience of the map – if the intended audience was residents of Staten Island, for example, it would be more appropriate to include it. In any case, this is an important design choice so the comment explains the rationale behind it. Map choices.

17

filter(precinct <= 119) keeps only those precincts outside Staten Island, since the Staten Island precincts all have numbers 120 and above (we could find this out by mapping all the precinct numbers). See Filtering rows.

18

Transform the precinct boundaries to the same CRS as the shootings. Matching CRSs is often useful when using multiple spatial layers together.

section: Step 6: Calculate and clip the density layer
text:
Step 6: Calculate and clip the density layer
## Wrangle data ----------------------------------------------------------------

# Calculate KDE
19shootings_kde <- shootings |>
20  hotspot_kde(
21    grid = hotspot_grid(precincts, cell_size = 400),
22    bandwidth_adjust = 0.33,
23    quiet = TRUE
  ) |>
24  hotspot_clip(precincts, quiet = TRUE)

19

Start with the shootings object we created and specify that we will store the finished density layer as shootings_kde.

20

hotspot_kde() estimates the density of crimes in each cell in a grid. The arguments on the following lines control how it does this. See Mapping crime density.

21

hotspot_grid() uses the precinct boundaries to define the grid that will be used to estimate the density of shootings. cell_size = 400 sets the cells to 400 metres across. That’s larger than we would usually use for a city map, but New York City is very large so a KDE layer with a smaller cell size would take a very long time to estimate. See Specifying a grid for kernel density estimation; Fine-tuning cell size and bandwidth.

22

bandwidth_adjust = 0.33 reduces the default smoothing bandwidth, relative to the default bandwidth value. Setting a value of bandwidth_adjust below 1.0 reveals more local detail, but more detail is not automatically a better representation: bandwidth changes the patterns a reader sees.

23

quiet = TRUE suppresses the progress display that is produced by hotspot_kde(). That reduces the amount of text output in the R Console, but means you might miss important messages. If you are running a long-running analysis, you might want to set quiet = FALSE to see the progress.

24

hotspot_clip() clips the density layer to the area covered by the precincts layer. That makes sure we don’t inadvertently show incorrect density estimates for grid cells that are outside the area that we have crime data for. See Clipping map layers.

26  shootings_kde,

29) +

26

27

The cartolight base map supplies geographic context with a relatively restrained appearance, helping the density layer remain prominent. See Base maps.

28

str_glue() from stringr allows us to combine multiple text values and R code into a single text value. The braces ({}) tell R to evaluate the code inside (today()) as R code rather than text, to insert the current date, while \n starts a new line. The caption credits the author and data providers, based on the information provided in the exercise instructions. Replace the example author name Joe Bloggs when producing your own map. What your map should show

https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/tempe_character_areas.gml
More details about the character areas data are available in the boundary dataset documentation.
Both datasets use EPSG:4326. Transform both layers to EPSG:6404, which uses metres and is suitable for analysing this part of Arizona. Acknowledge the City of Tempe as the source of both datasets under a Creative Commons Attribution licence.
